question.en: What are the current Core Web Vitals, and what user experience does each one represent?

answer.en: The current Core Web Vitals are **LCP**, **INP**, and **CLS**. LCP measures loading: when the largest image, text block, or video visible in the viewport renders. INP measures responsiveness across click, tap, and keyboard interactions, from the interaction until the next frame can be presented. CLS measures unexpected visual movement over the page lifetime. For a meaningful pass/fail discussion, use field distributions and the 75th percentile, segmented by mobile and desktop. Lighthouse is useful for diagnosis, but one lab run is not a substitute for what real users experience.

question.en: We already track FID in our dashboard, so our responsiveness story is covered, right?

answer.en: No. FID was replaced by INP as the responsiveness Core Web Vital (https://web.dev/articles/inp). FID only observed the input delay of the first interaction on the page, while INP observes the full duration of click, tap, and keyboard interactions, from the interaction until the next frame can be presented, across the whole page lifetime. A dashboard can show a healthy FID while real users suffer slow interactions that FID never measured.

question.en: Our median LCP is 1.9 seconds, so we pass the LCP assessment, right?

answer.en: Not necessarily. The Core Web Vitals assessment uses field distributions at the 75th percentile, segmented by mobile and desktop (https://web.dev/articles/vitals). A good median can coexist with a heavy tail: if enough loads are slower than the 'good' threshold, the p75 fails even though the median looks healthy. Report the distribution and check the p75 per segment.

question.en: How would you investigate and improve a poor LCP score on a product page?

answer.en: First identify the LCP element in field data and a trace; do not assume it is the hero image. Break the timeline into TTFB, resource-load delay, resource-load duration, and render delay. Then inspect the waterfall for late discovery, render-blocking CSS, client-side rendering or hydration, image dimensions and bytes, and font delays. Fix the largest measured phase: for example, make a critical image discoverable in HTML and correctly sized, or reduce server and render-blocking work. Re-run the same lab scenario, then verify the relevant route and device segment in RUM after release. Image compression alone is not a universal LCP fix.

question.en: We compressed the hero image by 60% and field LCP did not move. Why?

answer.en: Because image bytes only affect one of the four LCP sub-parts: resource-load duration. LCP time is the sum of TTFB, resource-load delay, resource-load duration, and render delay (https://web.dev/articles/lcp). If the dominant phase is slow TTFB, late discovery of the resource, or render delay (for example client-side rendering or hydration), compressing the image changes nothing. Identify the LCP element and split the timeline into the four phases first, then fix the largest one.

question.en: The LCP element turned out to be a text block, not the hero image. What changes about the fix?

answer.en: The image playbook stops applying. For a text LCP element, look at TTFB and render delay: render-blocking CSS, whether the text is server-rendered versus rendered or hydrated on the client, and font loading if the font swap changes what renders. The investigation still follows the same four phases, but the fixes move to server timing, CSS delivery, and rendering strategy.

question.en: What would you do when users report delayed clicks even though the page loads quickly?

answer.en: Start with field INP and identify the interaction, route, device segment, and phase that is slow. In a trace, separate input delay, event-handler processing, rendering, and presentation delay. Typical fixes are removing or splitting long synchronous tasks, reducing the DOM and render scope, avoiding forced layout, and moving non-UI computation to a worker when appropriate. Keep the first visual response small and immediate; debounce or defer only work that does not need to block feedback. TBT can help diagnose load-time main-thread blocking in the lab, but it is not a replacement for field INP because it does not observe real interaction behavior.

question.en: Lighthouse shows green Total Blocking Time, so INP must be fine. Right?

answer.en: No. TBT is a lab metric that sums main-thread blocking during the scripted load; it never observes a real interaction. Field INP can be poor even with green TBT because real users interact after load, on real devices, with handlers and layout work the lab run never triggers. TBT is a useful lab diagnostic for load-time blocking, but it is not a replacement for field INP (https://web.dev/articles/optimize-inp).

question.en: We made the click handler cheaper by debouncing it, and INP got worse. Why?

answer.en: INP measures from the interaction until the next frame is presented. Debounce delays the first visual response, which is exactly the portion of the interaction the metric observes. The pattern that works is to give immediate, small visual feedback (for example a pending state on the next frame) and defer only the work that does not need to block that feedback.

question.en: How do you prevent layout shifts in an asynchronously loaded feed?
The only layout shift on the page happens right after the user taps a button. Does it count against CLS?

answer.en: Possibly not. Shifts that occur close to a discrete user input like a tap, click, or key press can be excluded by the metric's rules; the layout-shift entry carries a hadRecentInput flag that marks these (https://web.dev/articles/cls). But the exclusion is narrow and defined: it does not cancel shifts from network responses, ads, or late fonts that happen to land after a click. Check the actual layout-shift entries rather than assuming, and do not use the exclusion as a reason to leave unrelated shifts unaddressed.

question.en: Lighthouse reports CLS 0 for the page, but support tickets say it jumps all over the place. How can both be true?

answer.en: A lab run loads the page once with scripted behavior and usually misses shifts that happen after the initial load: content injected on scroll, late embeds and ads, font swaps after interaction. Record layout-shift entries or use DevTools while performing the real user flow, and verify CLS in field data, because lab loading usually misses shifts that happen later in the page lifecycle (https://web.dev/articles/lab-and-field-data-differences).

question.en: What is the critical rendering path?

answer.en: It is the sequence of work needed for an initial render: parse HTML into the DOM, build the CSSOM, apply JavaScript that changes the DOM or CSSOM, create the render tree, calculate style and layout, paint pixels, composite overlapping pixels, and draw them. For the initial render, the browser generally needs part of the HTML plus render-blocking CSS and parser- or render-blocking scripts in the head; it does not normally wait for all HTML, images, fonts, or non-blocking scripts. The optimization goal is not to remove every resource, but to keep necessary first-screen work small and make non-critical work load later.

question.en: If we strip every render-blocking resource, first paint happens sooner. Isn't that strictly faster?

answer.en: No. For the initial render the browser needs part of the HTML plus the render-blocking CSS (and any parser-blocking scripts in the head); that is the work that makes the first paint meaningful. The goal is to keep necessary first-screen work small and make non-critical work load later, not to remove everything. Stripping all blocking CSS produces an earlier but unstyled paint, and the restyle when CSS arrives can move content and hurt LCP and CLS.

question.en: How do parser-blocking, async, defer, and module scripts differ for the critical path?

answer.en:
A classic script without an attribute pauses HTML parsing while it is fetched and executed, because it may mutate the document. `defer` lets downloading happen in parallel, preserves document order, and runs after parsing. `async` also downloads in parallel, but executes as soon as it is ready and does not preserve order, so it suits independent scripts. Module scripts are deferred by default. Choose based on dependency and ordering requirements, not a blanket rule: keep code required for the initial experience on the path, and defer analytics or other independent work. Then confirm the actual request and execution order in the Network and Performance panels.

```ts caption="Module scripts are deferred by default; an independent classic script can be async."
<script type="module" src="/app.js"></script>
<script async src="/analytics.js"></script>
```

question.en: Both scripts are async, and app.js calls globals defined in vendor.js. What breaks?

answer.en: Execution order. async scripts download in parallel but execute as soon as each finishes downloading, with no order guarantee. If app.js is smaller or on a faster connection, it can execute before vendor.js has run and throw a ReferenceError. Dependent scripts need defer (parallel download, document order preserved, execution after parsing) or module imports, which encode the dependency explicitly. Independent scripts like analytics are the right use for async.

question.en: Why doesn't our `type="module"` script need defer?

answer.en: Module scripts are deferred by default: they download in parallel and execute after HTML parsing completes, in document order. Adding defer to a module script is redundant, and avoiding modules because 'they block parsing' is based on classic-script behavior that does not apply.

question.en: How should you choose loading behavior for hero and below-the-fold images?

answer.en: Treat the likely LCP image differently from offscreen content. Make the hero discoverable early, serve an appropriately sized responsive source, preserve its dimensions, and avoid lazy-loading it when that would delay LCP. For images outside the initial viewport, `loading="lazy"` can defer network work until the browser considers them near view. Use responsive sources rather than sending a desktop-sized asset to every device, and optimize format and compression based on the actual display size. Validate the choice with a waterfall and LCP element; lazy-loading everything can delay content users need immediately. ```tsx caption="Keep the likely hero eager and dimensioned; defer a non-critical image." ```

question.en: We added loading="lazy" to every image including the hero, the audits look cleaner, but field LCP regressed. Why?

answer.en: Lazy-loading is a deferral, not a reduction. The likely LCP image now waits until the browser considers it near the viewport before its request starts, which directly delays LCP. Keep the hero eager, discoverable in the HTML, correctly sized with responsive sources and intrinsic dimensions, and apply loading="lazy" to below-the-fold images where deferred network work is a win.

question.en: The hero is a CSS background-image on a full-bleed section. Visually identical to an img tag, so same LCP behavior?

answer.en: No. An image referenced only in CSS is discovered after the stylesheet is fetched and parsed, so its request starts later than an image declared directly in the HTML, which the preload scanner can find immediately (https://web.dev/learn/performance/resource-hints). For a likely LCP element, make it discoverable in the HTML with an img or picture element and explicit dimensions; keep background-images for cases where the late discovery is acceptable.

question.en: How can web fonts affect LCP and CLS, and what is a responsible loading strategy?
We preloaded our self-hosted woff2 and it downloaded twice. Why would a preload cause a duplicate download?

answer.en: Fonts are fetched in CORS mode, even when self-hosted, so the preload must carry the crossorigin attribute and match the URL the CSS actually requests. A preload without crossorigin does not match the font request the stylesheet makes, and the browser downloads the file again (https://web.dev/learn/performance/optimize-web-fonts). The hint then wastes bandwidth instead of saving time.

question.en: font-display: swap, is that a free win with no downside?

answer.en: No. swap shows fallback text immediately, which helps when text is the LCP element, but the swap replaces text whose metrics usually differ from the web font, so the layout can shift when the font arrives, hurting CLS. The responsible setup limits families and weights to what the page needs, uses a compressed format (woff2), matches fallback metrics as closely as practical, and reserves space where appropriate, then verifies both LCP and field CLS.

question.en: When does code splitting improve performance, and when can it make a page slower?
We split aggressively and the entry bundle is tiny, but the route now feels slower to open. How is a smaller bundle slower?

answer.en: Because splitting moved cost from the entry to the load path of the task. If critical UI waits on a chain of tiny chunks fetched sequentially, the user pays a request waterfall that a single bundle would not have. A smaller entry bundle is not automatically a faster task when it adds late blocking requests; compare the initial waterfall, parse and execute cost, cache behavior, and interaction delay before and after.

question.en: Every route chunk bundles its own copy of the charting library. What went wrong with the splitting?

answer.en: The boundaries ignored the dependency graph. Naive per-route dynamic imports duplicate shared dependencies into each chunk, so users download the library multiple times across navigations and cache entries churn. Entry and shared-dependency splitting exist precisely to prevent duplication: extract the common library into a shared chunk that is downloaded once and cached (https://webpack.js.org/guides/code-splitting/).

question.en: How would you decide between preloading and prefetching a split chunk?

answer.en:
Use preload only for a resource needed during the current navigation and whose early fetch is justified; it competes with current critical work. Use prefetch for a resource likely needed by a future navigation, where idle-time bandwidth is acceptable. In webpack's model, a preloaded chunk starts in parallel with its parent and is fetched at a higher urgency, while a prefetched chunk waits until the parent finishes and is fetched during idle time. The decision must follow an observed user path and a waterfall, not a desire to fetch everything early. Measure whether the hint improves the next task without harming LCP or current-route bytes.

```ts caption="Webpack can emit a prefetch hint for a likely future module."
import(/* webpackPrefetch: true */ "./settings");
```

question.en: Why not just preload every chunk the page might possibly need?

answer.en: A preload is for a resource needed during the current navigation, and preloaded chunks start in parallel with their parent at higher urgency, so they compete for bandwidth with the current critical work, including LCP (https://web.dev/learn/performance/resource-hints). Preloading everything turns a prioritization hint into bandwidth contention. The decision must follow an observed user path and a waterfall, and be measured against LCP and current-route bytes.

question.en: Prefetch and preload are basically the same hint with different spellings, right?

answer.en: No. In webpack's model a preloaded chunk starts loading in parallel with its parent and is fetched at higher urgency, because it is needed during the current navigation. A prefetched chunk waits until the parent finishes and is fetched during idle time, because it targets a likely future navigation (https://webpack.js.org/guides/code-splitting/). Different scope, timing, and urgency: confusing them either delays current critical work (preload misused for future chunks) or spends idle bandwidth on the wrong resource (prefetch misused for current needs).

question.en: What does list virtualization solve, and what trade-offs must you account for?

answer.en: Virtualization, or windowing, renders only the visible slice of a large list and moves that window as the user scrolls. It limits DOM size, which can reduce rendering, style, and interaction work. It does not make each row cheaper, and it adds complexity: variable heights, scroll-to-item behavior, focus and keyboard navigation, screen-reader semantics, measurement, and testing need deliberate design. Overscan can reduce blank flashes during fast scrolling, but too much overscan gives back the DOM work. Profile first; use it when list size is a demonstrated bottleneck, and test accessibility and scrolling with the real data rather than treating virtualization as a default for every list.

question.en: We virtualized a 200-row list to fix slow row clicks and INP did not improve. Why?

answer.en: Virtualization limits DOM size, which reduces rendering, style, and interaction work that scales with the page's DOM. It does not make each row's handler or render cheaper. If the demonstrated bottleneck was the row's own work, or something else entirely, windowing changes nothing measurable. Profile first and use virtualization when list size is the demonstrated bottleneck, not as a default upgrade for every list.

question.en: We set overscan to 0 to keep the DOM absolutely minimal, and now fast scrolling shows blank rows. Why?

answer.en: With zero overscan, rows only render once they enter the viewport, and during fast scrolling the rendering cannot keep up with scroll velocity, so the user sees empty space until rows catch up. Overscan exists to render rows slightly beyond the viewport and cover that gap; too much overscan gives back the DOM work you were avoiding, so it is a tuning trade-off, not a maximization.

question.en: Why can a Lighthouse result disagree with Real User Monitoring, and how should you use both?

answer.en: Lab data is a controlled run with a chosen device, network, location, cache state, and scripted behavior. RUM is a distribution from real devices, networks, locations, browsers, cache states, and user actions. Therefore field users may have a different LCP element, later CLS, or interactions that the lab never performs. Use field data to prioritize user impact and segment the affected population; use lab traces to reproduce and isolate request, main-thread, rendering, or layout causes before shipping. For interaction work, TBT can be a useful lab diagnostic, but it is not INP. After release, compare the same route and segment in RUM.

question.en: CI Lighthouse says 98 but CrUX says the mobile segment fails LCP. Which number is the truth?

answer.en: Both are true for what they measure. Lighthouse is a controlled run with a chosen device, network, location, cache state, and scripted behavior; CrUX is a distribution from real devices, networks, locations, and cache states. The lab run can pass while the field population fails because they are different populations and scenarios. Use the field data to prioritize user impact and segment the affected population, and use lab traces to reproduce and isolate the cause before shipping.

question.en: We shipped the LCP fix today and CrUX still shows failure a week later. Did the fix not work?

answer.en: You cannot tell yet. CrUX data is a 28-day rolling average of aggregated field experiences (https://developer.chrome.com/docs/crux/api), so a fix shipped this week is diluted by up to four weeks of pre-fix data. Verify sooner with your own RUM at the 75th percentile for the affected route and device segment, and let CrUX converge over its window before judging.

question.en: What would a trustworthy field-performance measurement plan include?
We report vitals in the unload handler. Why are we losing a large share of samples?

answer.en: Because unload is not reliable for every lifecycle: mobile users frequently background the page or close the tab without an unload event firing, and lifecycle behavior differs across browsers. Send the data when the page becomes hidden (visibilitychange to hidden) as well as on unload, so a sample is captured the first time the page leaves the viewport.

question.en: We sum every layout-shift entry's value as our CLS, and our number is far higher than CrUX. Why?

answer.en: Because CLS is not a raw sum. The metric aggregates shifts into session windows and reports the largest window score, so many small unrelated shifts over a long visit do not simply add up (https://web.dev/articles/cls). Hand-rolled arithmetic also drifts on edge cases the reference implementation handles. Use the web-vitals library's onCLS, which implements the metric's defined aggregation rules, instead of recomputing the metric from raw entries.

question.en: How would you design performance budgets that a team will actually use?

answer.en: Tie a budget to a route, device class, and user task rather than choosing one global number. Combine quantity budgets such as initial JavaScript, image bytes, request count, and third-party cost with user-centric budgets such as LCP, INP, CLS, or task-specific long work. Set the budget from a measured baseline and product need, document the environment, and enforce it in CI for repeatable lab signals. Then monitor field distributions after release, because a passing synthetic budget can still hide a real-user regression. Give every exception an owner, expiry, and reason; otherwise teams learn to ignore a dashboard that only reports violations without helping prioritization.

question.en: Why is a single global budget, say 300KB of JavaScript for the whole site, the wrong shape?

answer.en: Because it is not tied to any route, device class, or user task. A marketing landing page and a data-heavy dashboard have different legitimate needs: the global cap either blocks necessary work on heavy routes or excuses waste on light ones. Tie budgets to a route and device class, combine quantity budgets (initial JavaScript, image bytes, request count, third-party cost) with user-centric budgets (LCP, INP, CLS), and set them from a measured baseline.

question.en: Every PR passes the CI budget checks, yet the field distribution regressed after release. How is that possible?

answer.en: CI enforces repeatable lab signals on a controlled scenario. A passing synthetic budget can still hide a real-user regression: different devices, networks, cache states, third-party behavior, or interactions the lab never performs. That is why budgets need field monitoring after release, comparing the same route and segment, with alerts against a baseline.

question.en: What is your workflow for diagnosing a janky interaction with Chrome DevTools?

answer.en: Reproduce the user flow with a representative device and throttled CPU, record the interaction in the Performance panel, and start with the screenshots, frames, CPU, and network overview. Zoom into the relevant time range, then inspect the main-thread flame chart and the Summary details. Look for long tasks, expensive event handlers, repeated style or layout work, forced reflows, large paints, and third-party activity. Select an event and follow its initiator back to source code. Change one cause at a time, record again, and compare both trace evidence and the user-facing metric. A profile is evidence about a scenario, not proof that every user has the same bottleneck.

question.en: You profiled on your development machine and found no long tasks, but users report jank. What is wrong with the trace?

answer.en: The scenario, not the finding. A trace is evidence about the scenario you recorded: a fast dev machine with a warm cache hides main-thread costs that real devices pay. Reproduce with a representative device and throttled CPU matching the affected field segment, then re-record. If users on low-end mobile report the jank, throttle to that class of device before concluding anything.

question.en: The trace showed one long task, we fixed it, users still complain. Why?

answer.en: Because a profile is evidence about one scenario, not proof that every user has the same bottleneck. Different routes, devices, and interactions can have different causes. Change one cause at a time, record again, compare both the trace evidence and the user-facing metric, and check field data for the affected segment to confirm the fix moved the number real users experience.

question.en: What is layout thrashing, and how would you fix it?

Nothing visually changed between frames, yet the trace shows Recalculate Style and Layout right before our getBoundingClientRect call every frame. Why is the browser recalculating layout it already computed?

answer.en: Because something wrote first. A style or DOM write earlier in the same frame invalidated the cached layout, so the geometry read cannot be answered from the previous layout and forces a recalculation. That is the forced-layout cost: it is not the read itself but the read landing after a write. Batch the reads before the writes, or cache the measurement, so the frame's geometry is queried once.

question.en: Should we ban all geometry reads like getBoundingClientRect to be safe?

answer.en: No. The goal is not to ban reads; it is to avoid forcing the browser to recalculate the same layout repeatedly within a frame. Batch reads before writes, calculate from cached measurements where possible, avoid querying layout inside large loops, and prefer transforms for movement. A single batched read per frame is fine and often necessary.

question.en: How would you govern resource hints and priorities across a large product?

answer.en: Start with ownership of the critical user journey and evidence from waterfalls and field metrics. Define a small set of allowed use cases: a preload must be required during the current navigation, a prefetch must represent a credible future path, and a connection hint must target an origin that is actually critical. Review hints as part of route changes because they compete for bandwidth and can become stale when design or navigation changes. Track hint count, duplicate downloads, LCP, initial bytes, and route-transition latency. Make the policy a design-system or platform concern, but keep route teams accountable for the user task; centralizing hints without route context is as risky as letting every team add them.

question.en: Why not have the platform team own every resource hint centrally? Wouldn't that stop teams from misusing them?

answer.en: Centralizing hints without route context is as risky as letting every team add them. A preload must be required during the current navigation and a prefetch must represent a credible future path, and those are route-level judgments a central owner cannot make reliably. The workable split is centralized policy (a small set of allowed use cases, review on route changes, tracking hint count, duplicate downloads, LCP, and route-transition latency) with route teams accountable for their user task.

question.en: How would you make performance a durable architectural property across many teams?

answer.en: Define performance as a product reliability concern with explicit journeys, owners, and field targets. Provide platform defaults that make the fast path easy: dimensioned media components, sensible font and script loading, route-aware splitting, accessible virtualization primitives, and a standard RUM schema. Enforce lightweight budgets and trace checks in CI, but use production percentiles to decide whether users improved. Establish a regression process that links a release, route, segment, metric, and rollback or owner. Govern third-party scripts and design-system changes because shared dependencies can affect every route. Architecture should reduce the number of teams that need to rediscover browser behavior, while preserving measurement and local accountability.

question.en: Every repo enforces budgets in CI and they are all green. Isn't performance now a durable property?

answer.en: Green CI is necessary but not sufficient. Durable performance is decided by production percentiles: whether users on real devices improved. Without a regression process that links a release, route, segment, and metric to an owner or rollback, drift accumulates invisibly, especially from third-party scripts and design-system changes, because shared dependencies affect every route at once.

question.en: When would you use PerformanceObserver, and what limitations should your measurement design acknowledge?
Our PerformanceObserver registers for an entry type but reports nothing for some pageviews even though the entries exist. Why?

answer.en: Because entries may have been recorded before the observer was created. observe() only delivers entries that happen after registration unless you opt into buffered observation, which replays already-recorded entries of that type. Register with buffered: true when the events of interest (long tasks, shifts, paints) may predate your script's execution.

question.en: Why not hand-roll the Core Web Vitals from raw PerformanceObserver entries and skip the library?

answer.en: Because the API is an input to a reporting design, not the metric itself. CLS needs its defined aggregation rules rather than a raw sum; INP has its own selection semantics across interactions; entries can arrive before observers exist (buffering); iframe content may be inaccessible to the top-level page; and unload is not a reliable reporting moment. A maintained reference implementation like web-vitals exists precisely to encode those rules, so prefer it and spend your effort on adding route and release context and reporting at visibility changes.
